newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: New Slovak securities law leaves analysts mixed.
newsitem.headline: New Slovak securities law leaves analysts mixed.

text.p: The Slovak parliament on Tuesday approved a new securities law forcing trading of registered shares onto accredited bourses.

But the law, which had been sent back to parliament by President Michal Kovac for revision, omitted a controversial clause which would have allowed major shareholders to arbitrarily cancel trade in an issue.
Despite the revisions to the law, which many feared could have disastrous effects on the equity markets in its original form, analysts were divided over the impact of the legislation.
"They approved the best version they could. The law will help improve transparency on the market and protection of minority shareholders," Peter Krutil, an analyst at Creditanstalt, told Reuters.

"We expect a positive impact among foreign investors, there are already first signs of their return, which could reverse the current downward market trend and bring higher trading activity," he added.
In addition to barring trading outside officially registered markets, the new law also forbids changes of registered shares into bearer shares, which was permitted under the previous law.

Martin Barto, an analyst at ING Barings, said he welcomed the scrapping of the controversial passages of the law, but warned that the positive effect should not be exaggerated since the market had many other ailments.
"The law is a positive signal, but there is much more behind the general bearish sentiment on the market and its decline," Barto told Reuters.
"We have to look at (the decline) from a wider perspective and take into account several other factors, such as some murky privatisation deals and lack of protection of minority shareholders."
These problems, analysts say, are at the heart of the Bratislava Stock Exchange's three-month-long slump which has seen the bourse lose some 25 percent.
Analysts add that an overseeing body such as a U.S.-style Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) would help lure back foreign investors by providing more market security.
